slides: Let's continue with working together, and see more ways to find the time together.

slides.say: There's another way, without fractions. We stretch the workers to the same time, and then we add the work.
Ella fills one bag of leaves in four hours. Tom fills one bag in six hours.
We can't add them yet, because the times are different. So we pick a time that works for both, twelve hours. Twelve divides by four and by six.
Four hours to twelve is times three. So in twelve hours, Ella fills three bags.
Six hours to twelve is times two. So in twelve hours, Tom fills two bags.
Now the times match. In the same twelve hours, together they fill three plus two, five bags.
at: together they fill three plus two

slides.say: We add the bags, not the hours, because they both work during the same twelve hours.
They want one bag. Five bags to one bag is divided by five. So the time is divided by five too. Twelve divided by five is two and two fifths hours.
A fifth of an hour is sixty divided by five, twelve minutes. So two fifths is twenty-four minutes.
So together they need two hours and twenty-four minutes.
We can also choose how big the job is. We pick a number that both times divide, so the rates are whole numbers.
Pipe A fills a tank in five hours. Pipe B fills it in twenty hours.
at: Pipe A fills a tank in five

slides.say: Let's say the tank holds twenty units, because five and twenty both divide twenty.
Pipe A fills twenty units in five hours. Twenty divided by five is four units an hour.
at: Twenty divided by five is four

slides.say: Pipe B fills twenty units in twenty hours. That's one unit an hour.
Together, four plus one is five units an hour.
Twenty units at five units an hour. Twenty divided by five is four hours.

slides: It's just like plugging in numbers. The tank's real size doesn't matter, so we choose an easy one.

slides.say: Before we calculate, we can often rule out choices. Here's how.
Together is always faster than the fastest worker alone. So it takes less time than the fastest worker needs.
And two workers as fast as the fastest one would need half his time. The other worker is slower, so together it takes more than that half.
at: two workers as fast as the fastest one

slides.say: Ella needs four hours, and Tom needs six. So together, less than four hours.
at: So together, less than four hours

slides.say: And more than half of four, two hours. Our answer, two hours and twenty-four minutes, is between them.
at: And more than half of four
Our answer, two hours and twenty-four

slides.say: And there's a short formula, only for two workers. We multiply the two times, and divide by their sum.
Ella and Tom, four and six hours. Four times six is twenty-four. Four plus six is ten. Twenty-four over ten is two and two fifths hours, the same answer.
Why does it work? It comes from adding the two rates. We don't need to prove it here.
Two equal workers, four hours each? Four times four is sixteen. Then four plus four is eight. Sixteen over eight is two hours. Half the time, as we expect.
Careful, the formula is only for two workers. With three workers, we add the rates.

slides.say: So let's sum it up. Working together, we add the rates, never the times.
A worker who works against the others gets a minus.
One job in four hours is a quarter of the job an hour.
Or we stretch the workers to equal times, or we choose a job size.
